sourceReviews.supportingSummary: I reread the lock-based and row-versioning sections. The unit distinguishes RCSI statement views from SNAPSHOT transaction views, requires ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION plus session selection, and describes dirty reads and SERIALIZABLE range protection. Its broad reader/writer no-blocking sentences are not approved; the product guide supplies schema-lock and first-access qualifications. Only the bounded read-only report claims are attested.

I inspected Isolation levels, Row versioning-based isolation levels and Behavior when reading data. The product documents statement versus transaction version selection, XSN establishment on first data access, Sch-S/Sch-M interactions, retained SERIALIZABLE locks and READ UNCOMMITTED dirty reads. It dates this row-versioning implementation to SQL Server 2005 and later. These passages support both the selected read view and the useful but different contexts of all alternatives.

choiceReviews.rationale: An intervening committed update can be visible to the next RCSI statement: the product says each statement selects versions using its newly sampled sequence boundary. That is useful for fresh committed reads per statement, but it does not provide the report’s common versioned view across all statements.

SERIALIZABLE can protect a stable read set through retained data/range locks, not the requested versioned read view. Those locks prevent conflicting updates from freely completing against the read set. It is appropriate when that locking is acceptable to enforce serializable access, but it does not meet this combination of requirements.

Supported, not incorrect: SNAPSHOT selects committed row versions from one transaction snapshot for the successive reads. The enabling option is supplied, and read-only ordinary data access avoids the shared data-read locks that would obstruct the relevant writers. First data access establishes the snapshot; neither schema-lock freedom nor write-conflict immunity is claimed.

READ UNCOMMITTED can read a writer’s uncommitted value that is later rolled back and can observe changing values across reads. Avoiding shared read locks does not construct a stable committed transaction snapshot. A deliberately approximate read that tolerates those anomalies is a different acceptable context.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: I reread both modifying-data branches. A SNAPSHOT update detects a concurrently committed row change and terminates on conflict; application handling/retry remains required even with optimized locking. Automatic RCSI/READ COMMITTED retry is explicitly a different branch. The read-version selection and transaction completion sections show why a new attempt cannot inherit the old transaction’s accepted context. These facts justify fresh read/calculate/write recovery, not blind replay of every business operation.

I inspected the multi-operation consistency discussion and SNAPSHOT subsection. They distinguish nonrepeatable observations, a common transaction view and same-row update conflict rather than silent overwriting. This supports rechecking a read-derived debit on a fresh attempt. The unit’s oversell narrative and universal no-blocking wording are not needed or endorsed; the product’s precise conflict contract governs.

choiceReviews.rationale: Supported, not incorrect: conflict ends the old SNAPSHOT transaction, so a retry must use a new attempt. Rereading and recalculating rebuild the debit’s input context after the competing commit instead of carrying an unvalidated old result forward. With no external effects and bounded retries permitted, this preserves the read-calculate-write unit without promising that every retry succeeds.

Waiting cannot resume a transaction terminated by a SNAPSHOT conflict, and the competing writer has already committed. Waiting is appropriate for a still-live transaction blocked on an active lock owner; it cannot make this failed transaction or its old computation valid again.

A new transaction alone does not validate the old read-derived UPDATE value. If an absolute remaining balance was calculated before a competing credit, blindly storing that value could discard the credit. A result independently known to remain valid could be reused under a different contract, but the stem supplies no such validation and this option expressly omits rereading.

An update conflict is failed validation of this write attempt, not acceptance of the intended debit. The product terminates that transaction. An uncontested SNAPSHOT write whose validation succeeds can commit normally, but this failed attempt has no accepted original debit to finalize.

Missing-index DMV column recommendations help formulate possible access-path improvements. They are recommendations, not a record of plan changes or a measurement of current operator rows. sourceReviews.supportingSummary: I read head-blocker tracing, sleeping uncommitted transactions, long-running-query tuning, short-transaction prevention and SQL Server system_health capture. The source distinguishes ordinary live blocking from circular deadlocks and victim recovery. The scenario uses those distinctions, not the flawed filtered-query example that purports to return a zero blocker, generalized XACT_ABORT promises or unconditional extra ROLLBACK code.

I inspected currently executing requests versus authenticated sessions and the plan/index diagnostic discussion. A request view reports executing requests while session inspection has wider scope; absence of an active request does not prove a committed transaction. Actual plan and index investigation can help costly access paths, but the supplied dependency chain determines the first transaction to inspect. No automatic index benefit is asserted.

I reread transaction completion and Discover long-running transactions. Commit or rollback completes a transaction and releases its resources; an application-controlled transaction can remain open while waiting for its user. The guide recommends identifying the owning user for appropriate completion/rollback and warns that KILL needs care. These support owner-coordinated investigation, not a blanket right for another connection to commit session 52 or automatically terminate production work.

choiceReviews.rationale: Execution-plan and index testing can help when a long-running statement’s access path holds too many locks. In this snapshot 61 is waiting on 58, so tuning 61 does not first locate the upstream transaction keeping the chain waiting. It may be worthwhile later without answering the immediate dependency question.

Shorter batches or a narrower predicate can reduce long lock retention when the targeted transaction is the relevant cause. Although 58 blocks 61, it is itself waiting on 52. Stopping at 58 therefore misses the next dependency; its batch design can be assessed after locating the upstream open transaction.

SQL Server system_health deadlock reports are legitimate evidence for recorded circular dependencies and victim recovery. This supplied snapshot instead points to a sleeping session with a still-open transaction. Historical victim analysis does not first locate that live transaction; the question does not claim no deadlock ever occurred elsewhere.

Supported, not incorrect: following 61 to 58 to 52 reaches the upstream session in the supplied chain. Its sleeping state and absent active request do not close the stated open transaction. Inspecting it with its application owner supports appropriate authorized completion or rollback, not automatic COMMIT, KILL or a claim every lock has already been proven.
